patient.key: 28F, 32 weeks pregnant, RLQ pain with nausea/vomiting, low-grade fever, leukocytosis with left shift

history.hpi: 28F G2P1, 32 weeks pregnant, presents to ED with abdominal pain. RLQ tenderness with rebound. Nausea and vomiting. Low-grade fever.
history.pmh: Uncomplicated pregnancy. First pregnancy: full-term vaginal delivery 4 years ago. Regular prenatal care. All prenatal labs normal. Anatomy US at 20 weeks normal.
history.social: Teacher. Enjoys reading and walking. ROS negative except GI as per HPI.

physicalExam.heent: Mucous membranes moist. Normocephalic. Pharynx normal. Neck supple.
physicalExam.chestLungs: Clear to auscultation and percussion. Equal chest expansion.
physicalExam.heart: S1/S2 normal. No murmurs, rubs, gallops. No JVD.
physicalExam.abdomen: Gravid abdomen consistent with 32 weeks. RLQ tenderness. Rebound tenderness present.
physicalExam.rectal: No rectal tenderness. No masses. Stool brown, no occult blood.
physicalExam.extremities: Trace bilateral lower extremity edema. No cyanosis, clubbing. Peripheral pulses normal.
physicalExam.neuro: Mental status normal. Cranial nerves, motor, sensory normal.

missed.why: Pre-surgery risk stratification. The patient is going to the OR — mandatory pre-op EKG.

missed.order: Type and screen / Type and Rh factor, blood
missed.why: Pre-surgery labs. Needed in case transfusion is required during or after appendectomy.
Patient has nausea and vomiting. Ondansetron is pregnancy-safe. Treat symptoms.
Patient has severe pain. Opioids are safe in pregnancy for acute pain. NSAIDs are CONTRAINDICATED in 3rd trimester (premature ductus closure, oligohydramnios). Acetaminophen insufficient alone.
Any pregnant surgical patient needs OB co-management for fetal monitoring and perioperative obstetric care.

Within 60 min before incision: cefoxitin + metronidazole OR cefotetan + metronidazole OR cefazolin + metronidazole OR clindamycin + (gentamicin or aztreonam). Coverage for GI flora — gram-negatives and anaerobes. Pregnancy category B only. NOTE: Zosyn (pip-tazo) and Augmentin are NOT accepted — too broad for surgical prophylaxis per ASHP/IDSA/SIS guidelines.

correctlyAvoided: CT abdomen/pelvis (radiation to fetus — significant deduction if ordered)
X-ray, abdomen (radiation to fetus — significant deduction if ordered)
All NSAIDs (ketorolac, ibuprofen, etc. — contraindicated >20 weeks: premature ductus closure, oligohydramnios, neonatal renal failure. FDA strengthened warning 2020)
Dextrose-containing IV fluids (D5W, D5NS, D51/2NS, D50W — causes fetal hyperglycemia → neonatal hypoglycemia; inappropriate for volume resuscitation)

errors.why: PT/INR was completely normal (10.5s, INR 1.0). No indication for FFP. Coagulation was intact.

errors.detail: Stayed in Emergency Department entire case. At simulated time 0 Days 00 Hours 15 Minutes, correct location was Inpatient Unit. Patient needs inpatient hospitalization for surgery and post-op monitoring.

scoreBreakdown.summary: 0 negative patient updates — treatment timing was excellent. Lost points on missed pre-op bundle (EKG, type/screen, antibiotics, OB consult, pain/nausea management) and wrong location (ED → Inpatient).

teachingPoints: Appendicitis is the most common non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy — 1 in 1,500.
First-line imaging in pregnancy = ULTRASOUND (no radiation). MRI without gadolinium if US non-diagnostic.
NEVER order CT or X-ray in a pregnant patient for abdominal pain.
NEVER give NSAIDs after 20 weeks gestation — premature ductus arteriosus closure, oligohydramnios.
NEVER give dextrose-containing fluids perioperatively — fetal hyperglycemia → neonatal hypoglycemia.
Pregnancy IS an absolute indication for appendectomy — antibiotics alone is contraindicated.
Pre-op bundle before any surgery: EKG + type/screen + PT/PTT + antibiotics within 60 min before incision.
Antibiotic prophylaxis for appendectomy: cover GI aerobes (cefazolin/cefoxitin) + anaerobes (metronidazole). Zosyn/Augmentin are too broad per guidelines.
Fetal monitoring before and after any procedure in a pregnant patient.
Transfer to Inpatient Unit, not surgery from the ED bay.
OB consult always accompanies any surgical procedure in pregnancy.
Treat nausea (ondansetron) and pain (opioids) — suffering is not diagnostic. NSAIDs are the wrong drug.

pathophysiology.appendicitis: Luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) → increased intraluminal pressure → venous congestion → ischemia → bacterial invasion → transmural inflammation → perforation if untreated.
pathophysiology.pregnancyDisplacement: The gravid uterus displaces the appendix superiorly and laterally. RLQ pain may be higher than expected. This makes the physical exam less reliable — imaging becomes even more important.
pathophysiology.pregnancyRisks: Delayed diagnosis → perforation → significantly increased maternal and fetal morbidity/mortality. Fetal loss rate with perforated appendicitis: 20-35% vs <5% with uncomplicated appendicitis.
